d: How the team finds investment opportunities: networks, inbound, intermediaries, thematic research, founder referrals. Proprietary sourcing (deals others do not see) is a claimed edge LPs test.
x: A VC fund sourcing 60% of deals from founder referrals.
A buyout fund using sector mapping to approach owners directly.
s: A GP claims proprietary deal flow.
LPs check how many deals were won without an auction.
Inbound volume rises but quality falls.

d: First filter on deals against the fund's mandate, stage, ticket size and thesis. Most deals are rejected here.
x: Of 2,000 inbound deals a year, 200 get a first meeting.
A credit fund screening for minimum EBITDA.
s: A great company outside the mandate.
Passing protects the strategy; referring it builds goodwill.
Screening by junior staff misses outliers.
Partners review a sample of rejections.

d: Investigation of a target before investing: commercial, financial, legal, technical, tax and ESG. Depth scales with ticket size and stage.
x: Quality of earnings report for a buyout.
Technical due diligence on a deep-tech startup's patents.
s: Price is cut, protections added or the deal dropped.
DD focuses on team, market and technology.

d: The written case for an investment presented to the investment committee: thesis, risks, valuation, terms and expected returns.
x: A 20-page memo with base, bull and bear cases.
A two-page seed memo.
s: The memo omits a key risk.
LPs ask to see memos in diligence.

d: A non-binding offer setting price and key terms, often with binding exclusivity and confidentiality. Precedes full due diligence and the SPA.
x: An LOI at 10x EBITDA with 60 days' exclusivity.
A non-binding indicative offer in an auction's first round.
s: The buyer lowers its price after diligence.
Allowed under a non-binding LOI, but it damages trust.
The seller can talk to other buyers.

d: A binding commitment by the seller not to negotiate with other buyers for a period, giving the buyer time to complete diligence.
x: 45 days' exclusivity after signing an LOI.
Exclusivity extended by two weeks.
s: The seller shops the deal during exclusivity.
Breach of the exclusivity clause; damages may apply.

d: A short, mostly non-binding summary of the main deal terms, signed before definitive documents are drafted. In VC it sets price, share class rights and governance.
x: A Series A term sheet based on NVCA templates.
A buyout term sheet with debt and equity terms.
s: A founder signs two term sheets.
Only one can proceed; reputational damage follows.
The term sheet is the reference for negotiation.

d: The binding contract for buying or selling a company's shares: price, completion mechanics, warranties, indemnities, conditions and limitations.
x: An SPA with a locked-box price and W&I insurance.
An SPA with an earn-out.
s: A warranty proves untrue after completion.
The buyer claims within limits; W&I insurance may pay.
Long-stop date in the SPA may let either side walk away.

d: The contract among shareholders governing the company after investment: board composition, reserved matters, transfers, drag and tag, information rights, exits.
x: An SHA giving the fund two board seats and veto rights.
A VC SHA with ROFR and co-sale.
s: A founder wants to sell shares.
ROFR and transfer restrictions in the SHA apply.
Majority wants to sell the company.
Drag-along in the SHA lets them force minority shareholders to sell.

d: Statements of fact by the seller or company about the business (accounts, contracts, tax, litigation) that give the buyer a claim if untrue, within agreed caps and time limits.
x: Fundamental warranties on title capped at price.
General warranties capped at 10% of price for 18 months.
s: Tax warranties or indemnity cover it.
Seller is a fund that wants a clean exit.

d: Insurance that covers losses from breaches of warranties in an SPA, letting the seller (often a fund) limit its liability and distribute proceeds sooner.
x: A policy covering 10% of enterprise value.
Buy-side W&I on a European buyout.
s: A fund wants to distribute proceeds without holdbacks.
W&I means the buyer claims against the insurer.
The breach was known to the buyer.
Known issues are excluded from cover.

d: Part of the price paid later if the business hits targets. It bridges valuation gaps but creates disputes over how targets are measured.
x: €20m upfront plus up to €10m on hitting revenue targets.
An earn-out based on EBITDA in years 1–2.
s: Buyer changes the business, missing the target.
Seller may claim breach of earn-out protections.
Fund must hold reserves or use a liquidating trust to receive it.

d: Two price mechanisms. Locked box fixes price at a past balance sheet date, with no leakage allowed after. Completion accounts adjust price for cash, debt and working capital at closing.
x: Locked-box price at 31 December accounts.
Completion accounts adjusting for net debt.
s: Seller pays a dividend after locked-box date.

d: A clause letting the buyer walk away if the target suffers a material adverse change between signing and closing. Courts set a high bar.
x: A MAC covering pandemic effects specifically.
A MAC excluding general market changes.
s: Usually not enough for a MAC; it must be durable and material.

d: Conditions that must be met before closing: regulatory approvals (antitrust, FDI), third-party consents, financing. A long-stop date sets the deadline.
x: Competition approval as a CP.
Foreign investment screening in France or India.
s: Closing slips; long-stop date may be extended.

d: Enterprise value is the value of the whole business, before deducting debt. Equity value is what shareholders receive: EV minus net debt and debt-like items.
x: EV €200m, net debt €80m, equity value €120m.
Debt-like items such as pension deficits deducted.
s: Buyer and seller agree EV but argue over debt-like items.
Equity value changes; the SPA defines items.
Equity value is a small slice of EV; small EV changes swing equity returns.

d: Enterprise value divided by earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. The most common pricing shorthand in buyouts.
x: Buying at 9x and selling at 11x EBITDA.
Software deals priced on revenue multiples instead.
s: Returns depend more on EBITDA growth.

d: Acquiring a company with a large share of debt secured on its cash flows. Debt boosts equity returns when things go well and magnifies losses when they do not.
x: A €300m buyout funded with €150m debt and €150m equity.
Debt at 5x EBITDA.
s: EBITDA grows and debt is repaid.
Equity value grows faster than EV.
Interest cost squeezes cash flow; covenants may tighten.

d: Existing managers reinvest part of their sale proceeds into the new structure, keeping them aligned with the buyer.
x: Founders rolling 30% of proceeds.
A CEO rolling €2m into topco.
s: Buyer insists on rollover to align incentives.
Should be on the same terms as the fund's equity, or disclosed.

d: Shares or options offered to managers at a low price, leveraged by the fund's preferred instruments, so they share disproportionately in upside.
x: Managers holding 10% of ordinary shares for a small investment.
A MIP vesting over four years.
s: Sweet equity multiplies; managers earn many times their investment.

d: The plan agreed at investment for how the business will grow and improve: hiring, pricing, add-ons, cost, systems. Tracked by the board.
x: A 100-day plan for a new buyout.
Annual value creation reviews.
s: Board resets priorities or changes management.
LPs ask for evidence of value creation.
GPs show the plan against outcomes.

d: Buying a platform company and adding smaller acquisitions, often at lower multiples, to build scale and earn a higher exit multiple.
x: A dental platform acquiring 20 practices.
Add-ons bought at 6x and exited at 12x.

d: Pre-money is the company's agreed value before new money; post-money adds the investment. Ownership acquired equals investment divided by post-money.
x: €4m into €16m pre-money gives €20m post-money and 20% ownership.
A SAFE with a post-money cap.
s: Founders bear the dilution; effective pre-money is lower.

d: The share class venture and growth investors usually buy, carrying rights such as liquidation preference, anti-dilution, protective provisions and conversion into common.
x: Series A preferred with 1x non-participating preference.
Growth equity convertible preferred.
s: Company sold for less than invested.

d: On a sale or liquidation, preferred holders receive a set multiple of their investment before common holders. Non-participating means they take either the preference or their pro rata share, whichever is larger; participating means both.
x: 1x non-participating is the market standard.
2x participating in a distressed round.
s: Company sells for €30m; investors put in €25m for 30%.
With 1x non-participating they take €25m rather than 30% (€9m).
Later rounds may rank senior; common gets little.

d: Adjusts the investor's conversion price if the company later raises at a lower price. Broad-based weighted average is standard; full ratchet resets to the new price and is harsh on founders.
x: Broad-based weighted average adjustment.
Full ratchet in a rescue round.
s: Down round at half the price.
Weighted average gives investors extra shares; founders are diluted.
Only investors who participate keep anti-dilution.

d: An investor's right to buy into future funding rounds so as to keep the same percentage ownership. It is negotiated in the term sheet or side letter, and it is why venture funds keep follow-on reserves.
x: A seed fund taking its pro rata in the Series A.
Major investor threshold for pro rata rights.
s: Pro rata rights secure a share.
It waives pro rata and is diluted.

d: A seat on the portfolio company's board, or an observer right, giving the fund oversight and influence.
x: Lead investor taking one board seat.
An observer seat for a smaller investor.
s: Board director owes duties to the company.
Conflicts with fund interests must be managed.

d: Matters that need investor consent, such as new senior shares, a sale, changes to the articles or large borrowings.
x: Investor consent needed for debt above €5m.
Veto over new share classes.
s: Company wants to raise a new round.
Preferred holders' consent may be required.
Investor uses veto to block a sale.

d: The investor's right to receive financial statements, budgets and other information from the company on a schedule.
x: Monthly management accounts and annual audited accounts.
Major investor threshold for information rights.
s: Breach of the SHA; investor can enforce.

d: A right for the company or existing investors to buy shares a holder wants to sell, on the same terms, before a third party can. ROFO (first offer) is a softer version.
x: Company ROFR on founder share sales.
Investors' secondary ROFR.
s: Founder agrees to sell to a secondary fund.
ROFR waived to allow a sale.

d: Lets holders of a set majority force the remaining shareholders to sell on the same terms.
x: Drag triggered by 75% of shareholders.
Drag requiring preferred majority consent.
s: Drag forces them on equal terms.
Liquidation preferences decide who receives what.

d: A shareholder agreement right that lets minority holders join a sale by the majority on the same price and terms, so they are not left behind with a new controlling owner. It is the mirror of drag-along.
x: Minority investor tagging along on a 60% stake sale.
Co-sale on founder secondary sales.
s: Investors may sell pro rata alongside.
Tag-along may force a larger purchase.

d: The record of who owns which shares, options and convertibles in a company, on a basic and fully diluted basis.
x: Fully diluted cap table showing a 12% option pool.
Cap table modelling a SAFE conversion.
s: Cap table plus preferences show payouts.

d: A financing at a lower price per share than the previous round. Triggers anti-dilution and usually a markdown in NAV.
x: Series C at 40% below Series B.
A flat round with extra terms.

d: The plan for number of companies, initial ticket sizes, reserves and sector or stage mix, built so the fund has a realistic chance of returning its target multiple.
x: 25 initial investments of €1.5m with half the fund held in reserve.
A buyout fund targeting 10–12 platforms.
s: Ownership too low for winners to return the fund.

d: LPA cap on exposure to one company, sector or geography, expressed as a percentage of commitments. SEBI caps Cat I/II AIFs at 25% of investable funds in one company (50% for LVFs).
x: No more than 15% of commitments in one company.
SEBI 25% cap for Cat II AIF.
s: The fund needs consent or a co-investment.
Limits usually apply at cost, not value.

d: EU Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation. Funds now disclose under Article 6, 8 or 9. The SFDR 2.0 proposal of November 2025 would replace these with Transition, ESG Basics and Sustainable categories; application is not expected before 2029.
x: An Article 8 fund promoting environmental characteristics.
An Article 9 climate fund.
s: A fund labelled Article 9 fails to evidence sustainable investments.
Reclassification to Article 8 and reputational damage.
Closed-ended funds created before application may be exempt under the proposal.

d: Considering environmental, social and governance factors in diligence and ownership, and reporting on them to LPs.
x: ESG diligence questionnaire for targets.
ESG Data Convergence Initiative metrics.

d: A contract, popularised by Y Combinator, giving the investor the right to shares at a future priced round, usually at a valuation cap and/or discount. No interest or maturity.
x: $500k on a $10m post-money cap SAFE.
A SAFE with 20% discount and no cap.
s: Company raises a Series A at $30m pre.
SAFE converts at the $10m cap, giving the holder more shares.
SAFE may never convert; holder has limited rights.

d: A loan that converts into equity at a future round, usually at a cap or discount, with interest and a maturity date.
x: €1m note at 5% interest, converting at a €8m cap.
Bridge note between rounds.
s: Holders may demand repayment or convert at a set price.
Accrued interest converts into extra shares.

d: The maximum valuation at which a SAFE or note converts. Post-money caps fix the investor's ownership; pre-money caps let it dilute with later SAFEs.
x: $10m post-money cap.
€6m pre-money cap.
s: Founders bear all dilution between SAFEs.
Conversion at the round price or discount.

d: A percentage discount to the next round's price at which a SAFE or note converts, rewarding early risk.
x: 20% discount to Series A price.
Discount or cap, whichever gives more shares.

d: A financing in which investors buy shares at an agreed price per share, setting a valuation, as opposed to convertibles.
x: A €10m Series A at €40m pre-money.
A priced seed round.
s: They convert at the priced round.

d: The sequence of venture rounds as a company grows, each with typical goals and investor types. Boundaries shift with market conditions.
x: Seed to prove product; Series A to scale go-to-market.
Growth rounds led by crossover funds.
s: A seed fund invests at Series A.

d: Shares reserved for employee options. Investors often require a pool of a set size in the post-money cap table.
x: A 10% post-money option pool.
ESOP top-up before Series B.
s: Unissued shares do not dilute payouts.

d: Creating or increasing the option pool before the round so the cost falls on existing holders, lowering the effective pre-money valuation.
x: €20m headline pre-money with a new 15% pool gives an effective €17m.
Negotiating pool size against the hiring plan.
s: Pool sized to a realistic hiring plan.

d: Shares or options earned over time, often four years with a one-year cliff, so people who leave early do not keep everything.
x: Four-year vesting, one-year cliff.
Founder re-vesting at Series A.
s: Before the cliff, they keep nothing.
Double-trigger acceleration on change of control and termination.

d: The fall in an existing holder's ownership percentage when new shares are issued. Normal in venture; value can rise even as percentage falls.
x: A founder going from 60% to 45% after a Series A.
Fund ownership falling from 15% to 10% without pro rata.

d: The harm to a company when a known existing investor declines to invest in its next round, which outsiders read as negative information.
x: A multi-stage fund passing on its seed company's Series A.
Seed programmes of large funds.
s: Some avoid large funds' seed programmes.

d: Short-term funding, often from existing investors, to reach a milestone or the next round. Can be positive (extending a winner) or defensive.
x: A €2m note from insiders to extend runway nine months.
An extension of the Series A at the same price.
s: Company needs time to hit metrics.
Signal the company struggles to raise.

d: A provision requiring existing investors to participate in a new round to keep preferred rights; those who do not are converted to common or lose anti-dilution.
x: Non-participating investors converted to common.
Pay-to-play in a down round.

d: Loans to venture-backed companies, often with warrants, used to extend runway with less dilution than equity. Repayment depends on future equity rounds.
x: $5m term loan with warrants for 1% equity.
Revenue-based financing.
s: Lender covenants or repayment add pressure.
Useful between rounds when growth is strong.

d: Rights to buy shares at a set price in future, often given to lenders or as sweeteners.
x: Warrants for 0.5% of equity attached to venture debt.
Warrants issued in a rescue round.
s: Company exits at a high value.

d: Founders selling some shares to new or existing investors, often alongside a round, to take money off the table.
x: A founder selling $2m of shares in a Series C.
Secondary sold to a growth fund.
s: Small secondaries are common and accepted.
Company and investors may buy first.

d: In venture, a small number of investments produce most of the returns. A fund's result depends on owning enough of its rare winners.
x: One company returning 3x the fund.
Top 10% of deals producing 80% of value.
s: A fund sells its best company early.
It may cap the fund's outcome.
Venture returns need exposure to outliers.

d: An investment whose proceeds alone equal the fund's size. VC managers test each deal for whether it could plausibly become one.
x: €10m stake exiting at €150m in a €150m fund.
Ownership targets set to make fund returners possible.
s: Company needs a huge exit to return the fund.

d: The stake a VC fund aims for at entry and after dilution, chosen so winners can move the fund's returns.
x: Seed fund targeting 10–15% at entry.
Series A fund targeting 15–20%.
s: Fund decides whether to accept lower ownership.

d: The investor who sets terms, writes the largest cheque, does most diligence and usually takes a board seat. Others follow on its terms.
x: Lead taking €6m of an €10m round.
Co-leads splitting a large round.

d: The group of investors in a round. Strong syndicates add capital capacity and networks; crowded ones complicate governance.
x: Three funds and two angels in a seed round.
An angel syndicate via SPV.
s: Weak insiders can hurt later rounds.
Lead invites a fund for its network.

d: An investor's right to require the company to buy back its shares after a set period. Rarely exercisable in practice but used as leverage.
x: Redemption after seven years at original price.
Redemption rights common in Indian deals.
s: Investor exercises but company has no cash.
Right may be unenforceable; negotiation follows.
Redemption rights used to force liquidity.
